s: Which one of the following most accurately describes the basic structure doctrine?
o: The Supreme Court alone may amend the Constitution when required
Only the Preamble can be amended subject to judicial approval
Parliament may amend every constitutional provision without limitation
Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features
x: The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
tq: Choose the precise statement distinguishing the amending power from its constitutional limitation.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the basic structure doctrine:
1. It is expressly defined in a separate provision of the Constitution.
2. It was developed by the Supreme Court through judicial decisions.
3. Its content has evolved case by case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The doctrine is not expressly defined in the Constitution. It is judge-made and its elements have emerged progressively through case law.
tq: Identify the false statement carrying the textual-definition trap.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s: With reference to the present position on constitutional amendments, which one of the following is correct?
o: Fundamental Rights may be amended only by an executive order
Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged
Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances
Fundamental Rights are outside the scope of Article 368
x: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, but the amendment remains subject to the basic structure limitation.
tq: Apply the rule to a specific constitutional component rather than recalling an isolated case name.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
2. The Preamble may be amended, subject to the basic structure limitation.
3. The basic structure doctrine means that only the Preamble cannot be amended.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and is amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine. Basic structure is not confined to the Preamble alone.
tq: Separate the true constitutional position from the restrictive ‘only’ formulation.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?
o: Supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
Supremacy of conventions over written provisions
Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts
x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
tq: Test the underlying constitutional principle rather than the name of the doctrine.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the Indian Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense?
o: Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power
The Constitution is written and supreme
x: Parliament does not possess an unlimited amending power. The written Constitution, Fundamental Rights, judicial review, federal division of powers and limited amending power restrict parliamentary sovereignty.
tq: Find the option that reverses a feature of the limited constitutional system.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s:
Assertion (A): The basic structure doctrine has been criticised as judicial rewriting of the Constitution.
Reason (R): The doctrine has no explicit textual definition and its content is developed by unelected judges case by case.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true. The absence of a textual definition and the open-ended judicial development of the doctrine form the basis of this criticism.
tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the criticism stated in the assertion.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s: Which of the following is regarded as a defence of the basic structure doctrine?
o: It checks majoritarian misuse of Article 368 and strengthens constitutionalism
It makes Parliament sovereign in the British sense
It permits majoritarian misuse of Article 368
x: The doctrine is defended as a major contribution of the judiciary to constitutionalism because it checks the misuse of the amending power by a temporary majority.
tq: Distinguish the stated defence of a doctrine from its criticisms and legal effects.
sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

s: The Supreme Court held in Shankari Prasad (1951) that:
o: The basic structure doctrine applies to all Ninth Schedule laws
Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights and an amendment is not law under Article 13
An amendment is law under Article 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights
x: Shankari Prasad held that Article 368 covers amendments to Fundamental Rights and that a constitutional amendment is not ‘law’ within the meaning of Article 13.
tq: Match the earliest case with its specific holding and avoid later-case attributes.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Sajjan Singh — first application of the basic structure doctrine
Golaknath — Fundamental Rights are transcendental and immutable
Shankari Prasad — 42nd Amendment provisions struck down
x: Golaknath held that Fundamental Rights were transcendental and immutable, treated an amendment as law under Article 13, and held that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights.
tq: Use the case-contribution pair and reject achievements belonging to later or different cases.

The Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971 and Article 31C
The Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 and Article 31A
The Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976 and Article 32

s: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on which date, under the Chief Justiceship of S.M. Sikri?
x: The judgment in Kesavananda Bharati was delivered on 24 April 1973, when S.M. Sikri was the Chief Justice of India.
tq: Distinguish the exact day and year from nearby constitutional dates.
sec: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

s: Which of the following propositions was held in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: The Preamble is outside the Constitution and cannot be amended.
The Preamble can be amended without any constitutional limitation.
The Preamble has overriding force over every constitutional provision.
The Preamble is part of the Constitution but can be amended subject to the basic-structure limitation.
x: Kesavananda Bharati held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable, but an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
tq: Discriminate between the Preamble being part of the Constitution and the limits on amending it.
sec: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

s: Who argued in India in 1965 that the amending power has implied limitations, drawing upon Germany's Basic Law?
x: German jurist Dietrich Conrad argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.
tq: Pair the jurist with both the year and the country from which the idea was drawn.
sec: Origin of the doctrine idea - jurist and country

s: The idea of implied limitations on constitutional amendment, which influenced the basic-structure doctrine, was associated with the constitutional experience of:
x: The idea was drawn from Germany's Basic Law, as explained by Dietrich Conrad in India in 1965.
tq: Test the country associated with the origin of the doctrinal idea rather than the Indian case that adopted it.
sec: Origin of the doctrine idea - jurist and country

s: Which one of the following is a Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrine?
o: Unlimited amending power under Article 368(4) and (5)
DPSP primacy over Articles 14 and 19 under Article 31C
x: Pith and substance is a judge-made interpretive doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court. The other listed propositions were associated with constitutional amendments enacted by Parliament.
tq: Separate judge-made interpretive doctrines from rules created through constitutional amendment.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Prospective overruling was evolved by the Supreme Court in which case?
x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was adopted by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
tq: Match the distinctive judicial doctrine with the case in which it originated.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The proposition that a constitutional amendment is not ‘law’ for the purpose of Article 13(4), and that Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights, was introduced by the:
x: The 24th Amendment inserted Article 13(4) and affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights through the constitutional amendment procedure.
tq: Distinguish neighbouring amendments by their specific constitutional consequence.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 25th Amendment gave primacy to the Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19 through Article 31C.
2. The 42nd Amendment widened the scope of Article 31C.
3. The widened form of Article 31C was fully upheld in Minerva Mills.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The widened Article 31C was struck down in Minerva Mills; therefore, statement 3 is false.
tq: Use the amendment sequence and the later judicial response to identify the false concluding statement.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Parliament's attempt to make its amending power unlimited and amendments non-justiciable was made through:
o: The 25th Amendment and the original Article 31C
The 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act
x: The 42nd Amendment inserted Articles 368(4) and 368(5) to declare amendments non-justiciable and the amending power unlimited. These provisions were struck down in Minerva Mills.
tq: Ask who created the power and which exact provisions expressed it.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down as violating the basic structure?
o: The provision giving effect to any Directive Principle an absolute priority over the Constitution
The provision creating the Ninth Schedule
The provision enabling Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights
The provision barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles
x: Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle. Judicial review was held to be part of the basic structure.
tq: Identify the precise judicial-review restriction rather than confusing it with the general objective of Article 31C.
sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following best expresses the constitutional significance of judicial review under the basic-structure doctrine?
o: Judicial review is available only when the President refers a question to the Supreme Court.
Judicial review may be removed by an ordinary law of Parliament.
Judicial review applies only to Fundamental Rights and never to amendments.
Judicial review is basic and cannot be removed even by a constitutional amendment.
x: Judicial review is itself regarded as a basic feature of the Constitution. Consequently, even a constitutional amendment cannot abolish it.
tq: Test the consequence of recognising a constitutional feature as part of the basic structure.
sec: Universal angles

s: The Supreme Court's recent position concerning the words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble is that they:
o: Were declared unconstitutional because they were inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
Were held to be enforceable Fundamental Rights in themselves.
Were removed from the Preamble by judicial direction.
Were upheld, and challenges to their insertion by the 42nd Amendment were rejected.
x: The Supreme Court upheld the words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble and rejected challenges to their insertion through the 42nd Amendment.
tq: Distinguish judicial validation of an amendment from striking down the amendment.
sec: Universal angles

s: The 75th anniversary of the First Constitutional Amendment, which created the Ninth Schedule, fell on:
x: The First Constitutional Amendment completed 75 years on 18 June 2026. It was the amendment that created the Ninth Schedule.
tq: Combine the anniversary figure with the exact date and identify the relevant amendment.
sec: Universal angles

s: The argument that voting should be elevated beyond a statutory right is linked in the contemporary basic-structure debate primarily with:
o: Democracy and free and fair elections as basic features
The primacy of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights
The basic feature of judicial independence alone
The immunity of all election disputes from judicial review
x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.
tq: Connect the proposed legal change with the basic constitutional features invoked to support it.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which of the following is a criticism of the basic-structure doctrine?
o: It is fully codified in an exhaustive constitutional list.
It is criticised as vague and unlisted, and as reflecting judicial supremacy.
It prevents every constitutional amendment without exception.
It was created directly by Parliament through Article 368(4).
x: Critics argue that the doctrine is vague, lacks an exhaustive constitutional list and may result in judicial supremacy. Supporters regard it as a shield protecting the Constitution from majoritarian excesses.
tq: Distinguish the criticism of indeterminacy from the supporters’ justification of constitutional protection.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which of the following statements regarding the debate on the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, is correct?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the Bill for violating judicial independence.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated before the JPC that the Bill did not violate the basic structure, while U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised doubts.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated that simultaneous polls necessarily violate the basic structure.
Former CJIs U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna rejected all basic-structure concerns about simultaneous polls.
x: B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.
tq: Match each public position with the correct constitutional office-holder.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which case is regarded as the first application of the basic-structure doctrine by the Supreme Court?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
x: The first application of the doctrine is identified with Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), where the relevant part of the 39th Amendment was struck down.
tq: Distinguish the case that formulated the doctrine from the later case that first applied it.
sec: Universal angles
